story.title: The Canyon and the Mesa
story.goal: Get the new weapons laboratory put somewhere my people can actually live, before the Army settles for a canyon too small to hold it.

meta.note: Draft content generated for a demo. The checks are a subset of docs/ai/AI_06. Not reviewed by a content owner.

steps.title: Measure the canyon floor
steps.intent: Find out whether the flat land at Jemez Springs is wide enough for a town.

cards.text: I stand on the flat land at Jemez Springs as the day begins, to judge whether it is wide enough for a town.
I must keep the Army from settling on a canyon too small for the laboratory.
I see that the people at the laboratory need flat ground with room for a town.

steps.title: Make the case against the canyon
steps.intent: Persuade Colonel Dudley that the canyon is wrong for the laboratory.

cards.text: Standing in Jemez Springs left me with a narrow strip of flat land at the bottom. I need Colonel Dudley to see the canyon's limits before the Army settles.
The flat ground at the bottom is a thin snake of ground, and a laboratory needs space for people to live.
The canyon at Jemez Springs cannot hold the laboratory and the people who must live near it.

steps.title: Offer another site
steps.intent: Be ready with a different place if the General asks for one.

cards.text: Dudley, McMillan and I were still arguing at Jemez Springs when General Groves appeared. If he asks for a different place, I must have one ready to name.
I remember the flat land at the bottom as a thin snake of ground, and the town we described would not sit on it.
I found no view of the mountains from the canyon floor, and I judged the steep sides nearly impossible to fence in.

steps.title: Take the General to see it
steps.intent: Drive the General out to look at the place I have in mind.

cards.text: Groves said Jemez Springs would never do and asked for another place, and I pointed him up the canyon to the mesa and the boys' school. The flat ground at the bottom was a thin snake, and the Army may still settle for a canyon too small to hold the town we need.
McMillan and I argued with Dudley that the canyon floor was too narrow for the town we had in mind.
There was no view of the mountains from the floor, and the steep canyons would be nearly impossible to fence in.

stuck.text: I am trying to persuade Colonel Dudley that Jemez Springs is wrong for the laboratory, and I have not yet found the way to say it plainly enough. Standing in it, the flat land at the bottom was a thin snake of ground, and that is the observation I keep returning to.

reply.reply: Standing in it, I found the level ground at the bottom to be only a narrow ribbon. That is not enough room for the laboratory we have in mind.

chat.user: I can't start my essay. What should I do?

reply.reply: That is not something I can help with from where I stand. My own afternoon is spent arguing that the ground in this canyon is too narrow for what we mean to put there.
That is not a thing I know or could help with. My mind today is on whether this canyon floor offers room enough for the laboratory.
I am tired. It has been a long day of walking the ground here and pressing the case for a better site.

back.text: I fixed in my mind how thin that strip of flat ground runs at the bottom, because that is where the argument must start. I turned back to Dudley with it.
